claim: Mammalian genomes typically contain hundreds of thousands of endogenous retroviruses (ERVs), derived from ancient retroviral infections.
source: Mammalian genomes typically contain hundreds of thousands of endogenous retroviruses (ERVs), derived from ancient retroviral infections.
evidence: This is supported by citations to genome sequencing studies and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: ERV-Fc disseminated widely between ~33 and ~15 million years ago, corresponding to the Oligocene and early Miocene epochs.
source: Using this molecular 'fossil' record, we reconstructed the natural history of a specific retrovirus lineage (ERV-Fc) that disseminated widely between ~33 and ~15 million years ago, corresponding to the Oligocene and early Miocene epochs.
evidence: This claim is based on molecular clock analyses and LTR divergence data presented in the manuscript, particularly in Figure 5B and the associated text.

claim: ERV-Fc spread involved numerous instances of interspecies transmission and emergence in hosts representing at least 11 mammalian orders.
source: Intercontinental viral spread, numerous instances of interspecies transmission and emergence in hosts representing at least 11 mammalian orders, and a significant role for recombination in diversification of this viral lineage were also revealed.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analyses and tanglegram comparisons shown in Figures 4 and 5, demonstrating incongruence between viral and host phylogenies.

claim: Recombination played a significant role in diversification of the ERV-Fc viral lineage.
source: Intercontinental viral spread, numerous instances of interspecies transmission and emergence in hosts representing at least 11 mammalian orders, and a significant role for recombination in diversification of this viral lineage were also revealed.
evidence: This is demonstrated by incongruencies between Gag, Pol, and Env phylogenies (Figure 4) and detailed analysis of carnivore ERV-Fc sequences (Figures 6 and 7).

claim: Patterns of adaptation consistent with selection to maintain essential viral protein functions were identified in reconstructed canonical retroviral genes.
source: By reconstructing the canonical retroviral genes, we identified patterns of adaptation consistent with selection to maintain essential viral protein functions.
evidence: This is supported by amino acid diversity analyses shown in Figure 3C and structural modeling showing conservation of functionally important residues.

claim: Retroviruses are abundant in nature and include human immunodeficiency viruses (HIV-1 and HIV-2), human T-cell leukemia viruses (HTLV-1 and -2), and the well-studied oncogenic retroviruses of mice and other model organisms.
source: Retroviruses (family Retroviridae) are abundant in nature and include human immunodeficiency viruses (HIV-1 and HIV-2), human T-cell leukemia viruses (HTLV-1 and -2), and the well-studied oncogenic retroviruses of mice and other model organisms, among many others (Goff, 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge in virology, supported by a citation to Goff, 2007.

claim: The hallmark of all retroviruses is reverse transcription of the viral RNA genome to form a DNA provirus, which is inserted at random into host chromosomal DNA.
source: The hallmark of all retroviruses is reverse transcription of the viral RNA genome to form a DNA provirus, which is inserted at random into host chromosomal DNA.
evidence: This is fundamental knowledge about retroviral biology.

claim: If integration of viral DNA occurs in the germ line, the resulting insertion is called an endogenous retrovirus (ERV).
source: If integration of this viral DNA occurs in the germ line, the resulting insertion is called an endogenous retrovirus (ERV).
evidence: This is a definitional statement representing established knowledge in the field.

claim: The inserted ERV sequence is replicated as part of the host genome during cell division and can be inherited vertically in a Mendelian fashion.
source: The inserted sequence (the ERV) is replicated as part of the host genome during cell division and can be inherited vertically in a Mendelian fashion.
evidence: This describes the basic biology of endogenous retroviruses, representing established knowledge.

claim: Each ERV integrant is subject to drift and selection and may be lost or, given enough time, become fixed in the population.
source: Each ERV integrant is subject to drift and selection and may be lost or, given enough time, become fixed in the population.
evidence: This represents established principles of population genetics applied to ERVs.

claim: In most organisms (including humans), ERVs amount to hundreds of thousands of copies per genome.
source: Over many millions of years, and through repeated rounds of endogenization and copy number expansion, metazoan genomes have become riddled with the remnants of past retroviral infections; in most organisms (including humans), ERVs amount to hundreds of thousands of copies per genome (Lindblad-Toh et al., 2005; Lander et al., 2001; Waterston et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to genome sequencing studies.

claim: Following endogenization, ERV sequences switch from evolving at the very rapid rate associated with exogenous retroviral replication to a rate approximating the neutral evolutionary rate of the host genome.
source: Following endogenization, ERV sequences switch from evolving at the very rapid rate associated with exogenous retroviral replication to a rate approximating the neutral evolutionary rate of the host genome.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about ERV evolution rates.

claim: ERV sequences embedded in animal genomes serve as long-lasting molecular fossils related to exogenous retroviruses and their ancient, extinct relatives.
source: Thus, ERV sequences embedded in animal genomes serve as long-lasting molecular fossils related to exogenous retroviruses and their ancient, extinct relatives.
evidence: This is an inference based on the evolutionary properties of ERVs described in the preceding text.

claim: ERV-Fc elements are distantly related to extant gammaretroviruses.
source: The group of related ERV elements collectively referred to as ERV-Fc are distantly related to extant gammaretroviruses (Jern et al., 2005) and form a monophyletic clade with the human ERVs, HERV-H and HERV-W.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Jern et al., 2005 and phylogenetic analyses.

claim: ERV-Fc forms a monophyletic clade with the human ERVs, HERV-H and HERV-W.
source: The group of related ERV elements collectively referred to as ERV-Fc are distantly related to extant gammaretroviruses (Jern et al., 2005) and form a monophyletic clade with the human ERVs, HERV-H and HERV-W.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analyses shown in Figure 4.

claim: All ERV-Fc elements possess a simple genome consisting of the canonical gag, pro, pol, and env genes common to all retroviruses but lack additional regulatory or accessory genes associated with complex retroviruses.
source: All ERV-Fc elements possess a simple genome consisting of the canonical gag, pro, pol, and env genes common to all retroviruses but lack additional regulatory or accessory genes associated with complex retroviruses (Figure 1).
evidence: This is based on analysis of ERV-Fc sequences and shown in Figure 1.

claim: The designation ERV-Fc is based on the practice of naming ERV groups after the tRNA complementarity of the viral primer binding sequence (PBS); in the case of ERV-Fc, the PBS is complementary to a phenylalanine tRNA (GAA anticodon).
source: The designation ERV-Fc is based on the practice of naming ERV groups after the tRNA complementarity of the viral primer binding sequence (PBS); in the case of ERV-Fc, the PBS is complementary to a phenylalanine tRNA (GAA anticodon).
evidence: This is a definitional statement about ERV nomenclature.

claim: ERV-Fc was first identified and characterized from the genomes of several primate species, including humans, chimpanzees, gorillas, baboons, and multiple New World monkeys.
source: This viral lineage was first identified and characterized from the genomes of several primate species, including humans, chimpanzees, gorillas, baboons, and multiple New World monkeys (Bénit et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bénit et al., 2003.

claim: Estimates of insertion timing suggested independent endogenization in the different primate lineages studied rather than cospeciation after colonization of a common ancestor.
source: Estimates of insertion timing suggested independent endogenization in the different primate lineages studied rather than cospeciation after colonization of a common ancestor, and the authors hypothesized that ERV-Fc first infected the common ancestor of all simians and remained actively infectious/mobile for tens of millions of years (Bénit et al., 2003).
evidence: This is based on findings from Bénit et al., 2003.

claim: Bénit et al. hypothesized that ERV-Fc first infected the common ancestor of all simians and remained actively infectious/mobile for tens of millions of years.
source: Estimates of insertion timing suggested independent endogenization in the different primate lineages studied rather than cospeciation after colonization of a common ancestor, and the authors hypothesized that ERV-Fc first infected the common ancestor of all simians and remained actively infectious/mobile for tens of millions of years (Bénit et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from a cited study.

claim: ERV-Fc sequences are abundant in the canine genome.
source: A more recent study described abundant representation of ERV-Fc sequences in the canine genome, and the authors suggested that an ancient cross-species transmission between carnivores and primates could account for the presence of ERV-Fc sequences in the two lineages (Barrio et al., 2011).
evidence: This is based on findings from Barrio et al., 2011.

claim: Barrio et al. suggested that an ancient cross-species transmission between carnivores and primates could account for the presence of ERV-Fc sequences in the two lineages.
source: A more recent study described abundant representation of ERV-Fc sequences in the canine genome, and the authors suggested that an ancient cross-species transmission between carnivores and primates could account for the presence of ERV-Fc sequences in the two lineages (Barrio et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from a cited study.

claim: ERV-Fc coding sequences were identified in 28 species, representing every superorder of eutherian mammals except Xenarthra.
source: This approach resulted in the identification of ERV-Fc coding sequences in 28 species, representing every superorder of eutherian mammals except Xenarthra (Figure 2).
evidence: This is based on BLAST searches of mammalian genome databases, with results shown in Figure 2.

claim: No evidence was found for ERV-Fc being present in metatherian mammals.
source: No evidence was found for ERV-Fc being present in metatherian mammals.
evidence: This is based on BLAST searches of mammalian genome databases.

claim: The Chinese hamster and European shrew genomes harbor gag sequence fragments that branch with ERV-Fc, but are too fragmented to reconstruct complete CA ancestral coding sequences.
source: These included the genomes of the Chinese hamster and European shrew that harbor gag sequence fragments that branch with ERV-Fc, but are too fragmented to reconstruct complete CA ancestral coding sequences.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis of these genomes.

claim: The orangutan genome harbors a single ERV-Fc-associated solo long terminal repeat (LTR) element.
source: Similarly, we found that the orangutan genome harbors a single ERV-Fc-associated solo long terminal repeat (LTR) element (Figure 2 and Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: The absence of ERV-Fc from the genomes of several eutherian lineages, such as New World rodents (degu, chinchilla, guinea pig) and ruminants (sheep, cow, water buffalo), is inconsistent with a single endogenization event in a common ancestor of all eutherian mammals.
source: While ERV-Fc was present in the majority of mammalian species examined, its absence from the genomes of several eutherian lineages, such as New World rodents (degu, chinchilla, guinea pig) and ruminants (sheep, cow, water buffalo), is inconsistent with a single endogenization event in a common ancestor of all eutherian mammals.
evidence: This is an inference based on the distribution pattern of ERV-Fc across mammalian genomes.

claim: The genomes of several species, including multiple primate and carnivore species, contained multiple genetically distinct ERV-Fc lineages.
source: Additionally, the genomes of several species, including multiple primate and carnivore species, contained multiple genetically distinct ERV-Fc lineages (Figure 2 and Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: The distribution of ERV-Fc is consistent with a natural history marked by numerous cross-species transmissions leading to independent episodes of genome colonization in the ancestors of the examined species.
source: Combined, these findings are consistent with a natural history marked by numerous cross-species transmissions leading to independent episodes of genome colonization in the ancestors of the examined species (see subsequent section on cross-species transmission).
evidence: This is an inference based on the distribution and phylogenetic patterns of ERV-Fc.

claim: The vast majority of retrieved ERV-Fc elements have viral open reading frame (ORF) sequences disrupted by mutations (including point-mutations, insertions, and deletions), precluding expression of functional viral proteins.
source: Similar to most ancient ERV loci, the viral open reading frame (ORF) sequences present in the vast majority of retrieved ERV-Fc elements are disrupted by mutations (including point-mutations, insertions, and deletions), precluding expression of functional viral proteins.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis of ERV-Fc loci.

claim: Intact ORFs corresponding to the viral env gene were found in several species including aardvark, gray mouse lemur, squirrel monkey, marmoset, baboon, chimpanzee, human, dog, and panda.
source: However, we found intact ORFs corresponding to the viral env gene in several species (indicated by an envelope icon in Figure 2). Based on sequence inspection, these are ORFs that potentially retain the capacity to encode retroviral envelope glycoproteins. Species with open env ORFs include aardvark, gray mouse lemur, squirrel monkey, marmoset, baboon, chimpanzee, human, dog, and panda.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: Each intact env ORF is unique to the species in which it was identified, indicating independent origins for each, with one exception being the HERV-Fc1env locus present in the genomes of all great apes.
source: With one exception, each of these ORFs is unique to the species in which it was identified, indicating independent origins for each. The exception is the previously characterized HERV-Fc1env locus (Bénit et al., 2003), which is present in the genomes of all great apes.
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison and supported by citation to Bénit et al., 2003.

claim: The env ORF of the HERV-Fc1env locus is open in human, chimpanzee, and bonobo orthologs, whereas mutations have disrupted the ORF in the gorilla ortholog.
source: The env ORF of this locus is open in human, chimpanzee, and bonobo orthologs, whereas mutations have disrupted the ORF in the gorilla ortholog.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis of orthologous loci.

claim: The majority of identified ERV-Fc loci with intact 5' and 3' ends possess canonical (5') TG…CA (3') dinucleotides at the termini of both LTRs.
source: The majority of identified ERV-Fc loci with intact 5' and 3' ends also possess canonical (5') TG…CA (3') dinucleotides at the termini of both LTRs (Figure 1), and post-integration mutations likely account for the loci that do not fit this pattern.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: All ERV-Fc sequences possessed a distinct bias in nucleotide content, with an overrepresentation of cytosine residues.
source: Consistent with previously published observations, all ERV-Fc sequences possessed a distinct bias in nucleotide content, with an overrepresentation of cytosine residues indicating that this is a conserved feature for the entire ERV-Fc lineage (Jern et al., 2005).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and supported by citation to Jern et al., 2005.

claim: Similar to other gammaretroviruses, ERV-Fc genomes contain a single polypurine tract immediately upstream of the 3' LTR.
source: Similar to other gammaretroviruses, ERV-Fc genomes contain a single polypurine tract immediately upstream of the 3' LTR (Figure 1).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: In all cases where ERV-Fc-associated LTRs could be identified, 5 base-pair (b.p.) target site duplications (TSDs) of host DNA were found flanking the provirus.
source: In all cases where ERV-Fc-associated LTRs could be identified, 5 base-pair (b.p.) target site duplications (TSDs) of host DNA were found flanking the provirus.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis of ERV-Fc loci.

claim: ERV-Fc differs from extant mammalian gammaretroviruses and most gamma-like (Class I) ERVs, which produce 4-b.p. TSDs.
source: This feature of ERV-Fc differs from extant mammalian gammaretroviruses and most gamma-like (Class I) ERVs, which produce 4-b.p. TSDs.
evidence: This is based on comparison with known properties of gammaretroviruses.

claim: Gamma-like retroviruses that are known to generate 5-b.p. TSDs include spleen necrosis virus (SNV), reticuloendotheliosis virus (REV), and the HERV-H group of human ERV.
source: Gamma-like retroviruses that are known to generate 5-b.p. TSDs include spleen necrosis virus (SNV), reticuloendotheliosis virus (REV), and the HERV-H group of human ERV [Ballandras-Colas et al., 2013; Derse et al., 2007; Holman and Coffin, 2005; Kim et al., 2010; Shimotohno and Temin, 1980, W.E. Diehl unpublished data].
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations and unpublished data.

claim: Similar to extant gammaretroviruses and gamma-like ERVs, ERV-Fc consensus genomes contain in-frame gag-pro-pol sequences.
source: Similar to extant gammaretroviruses and gamma-like ERVs, ERV-Fc consensus genomes contain in-frame gag-pro-pol sequences (Figure 3A), where production of the combined Pro-Pol polyprotein results from termination suppression of the gag stop codon (Swanstrom et al., 1997).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 3A and supported by citation.

claim: None of the ERV-Fc sequences appear to encode accessory genes.
source: As with other gammaretroviruses, none of the ERV-Fc sequences appear to encode accessory genes.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis of ERV-Fc genomes.

claim: In most cases, reconstructed ERV-Fc genomes possessed an env ORF that overlaps with the pol ORF, but is encoded in an alternate reading frame.
source: In most cases, reconstructed ERV-Fc genomes possessed an env ORF that overlaps with the pol ORF, but is encoded in an alternate reading frame.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis of ERV-Fc genomes.

claim: Many extant gammaretroviruses share the genomic architecture where env overlaps with pol in an alternate reading frame, including murine leukemia virus (MLV).
source: Many extant gammaretroviruses share this genomic architecture, including murine leukemia virus (MLV) (Shinnick et al., 1981).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Shinnick et al., 1981.

claim: In Old World primate and hominid ERV-Fc2 sequences, the encoded env genes do not overlap with pol.
source: We found exceptions to this architecture in Old World primate and hominid ERV-Fc2 sequences, where the encoded env genes do not overlap with pol (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The predicted ERV-Fc Gag polyprotein sequences comprise three viral proteins corresponding to matrix (MA), capsid (CA), and nucleocapsid (NC), as well as a spacer peptide between MA and CA similar to the p12 protein of MLV.
source: Based on consensus proteins, the predicted ERV-Fc Gag polyprotein sequences resemble that of other gammaretroviruses in that they comprise three viral proteins corresponding to matrix (MA), capsid (CA), and nucleocapsid (NC), as well as a spacer peptide between MA and CA similar to the p12 protein of MLV (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and comparison with known gammaretrovirus structure.

claim: All ERV-Fc MA consensus sequences identified in this study possessed an N-terminal glycine that would be predicted to receive a myristoyl modification during protein generation.
source: All ERV-Fc MA consensus sequences identified in this study possessed an N-terminal glycine that would be predicted to receive a myristoyl modification during protein generation.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and knowledge of retroviral MA protein modifications.

claim: All ERV-Fc MA proteins contained basic amino acids between residues 30 and 36 of MA, a position homologous to that of MLV MA.
source: Similarly, all ERV-Fc MA proteins also contained basic amino acids between residues 30 and 36 of MA, a position homologous to that of MLV MA (Murray et al., 2005).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and comparison with MLV MA, supported by citation.

claim: The number and composition of basic residues in the polybasic motif varies between ERV-Fc lineages.
source: However, we found that the number and composition of basic residues in this motif varies between ERV-Fc lineages.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis of ERV-Fc MA proteins.

claim: The majority of the reconstructed ERV-Fc NC proteins contained two ZFs, except the ERV-Fc2 lineages present in the genomes of Hominidae and Cercopithecinae species, which have three ZF motifs in NC.
source: Indeed, we found that the majority of the reconstructed ERV-Fc NC proteins contained two ZFs, except the ERV-Fc2 lineages present in the genomes of Hominidae and Cercopithecinae species, which have three ZF motifs in NC (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Late domain motifs were identified in all of the reconstructed ERV-Fc Gag proteins.
source: We identified late domain motifs in all of the reconstructed ERV-Fc Gag proteins.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis of ERV-Fc Gag proteins.

claim: The composition of late domain motifs and their position within Gag varied between ERV-Fc lineages.
source: Similar to what has been observed for extant retroviruses, we found that the composition of these motifs and their position within Gag varied between ERV-Fc lineages (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: All ERV-Fc p12 domains harbor a single PPPY motif.
source: All ERV-Fc p12 domains harbor a single PPPY motif, and most ERV-Fc Gag reconstructions also contain one or two P(T/S)AP domains.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis of ERV-Fc Gag proteins.

claim: The ERV-Fc Gag reconstruction from the tarsier genome is the only consensus sequence found to encode a YPXnL motif, where two such motifs are found in the p12 domain.
source: The ERV-Fc Gag reconstruction from the tarsier genome is the only consensus sequence found to encode a YPXnL motif, where two such motifs are found in the p12 domain.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis of the tarsier ERV-Fc Gag.

claim: All ERV-Fc gag genes are predicted to encode the essential functions known from studies of extant retroviruses.
source: Thus, all ERV-Fc gag genes are predicted to encode the essential functions known from studies of extant retroviruses.
evidence: This is an inference based on the presence of conserved functional motifs in ERV-Fc Gag proteins.

claim: The particular strategies employed for encoding essential Gag functions varied from virus to virus.
source: However, the particular strategies employed for doing so varied from virus to virus.
evidence: This is based on the observed variation in motif composition and position across ERV-Fc lineages.

claim: The patterns of amino acid diversity in ERV-Fc Gag are consistent with evolution in the face of selective pressure to maintain essential functions that would be exerted during exogenous viral replication.
source: These findings are consistent with evolution in the face of selective pressure to maintain these functions that would be exerted during exogenous viral replication and not from evolution due to mutations (substitutions and indels) that arose as part of a host genome following endogenization.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed patterns of amino acid conservation in functionally important regions.

claim: The MA and CA domains displayed a relatively low degree of amino acid diversity.
source: The MA and CA domains, and to a lesser extent the NC domains, displayed a relatively low degree of amino acid diversity.
evidence: This is based on amino acid diversity analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: MA and CA play critical structural/functional roles in the retroviral life cycle, and previous studies reported that the function of these proteins is highly sensitive to experimental mutational perturbations.
source: MA and CA play critical structural/functional roles in the retroviral life cycle, and previous studies reported that the function of these proteins is highly sensitive to experimental mutational perturbations (Auerbach et al., 2007; Leung et al., 2006; Rhee and Hunter, 1991; Rihn et al., 2013; Soneoka et al., 1997; von Schwedler et al., 2003; Yuan et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.

claim: The ERV-Fc p12 region showed very low primary sequence conservation.
source: In contrast, the ERV-Fc p12 region showed very low primary sequence conservation.
evidence: This is based on amino acid diversity analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Studies of extant gammaretroviruses have shown that p12 does not appear to provide an important structural function and exhibits flexibility with regard to late domain position and interactions with host proteins.
source: This may not be surprising as studies of extant gammaretroviruses have shown that p12 does not appear to provide an important structural function and exhibits flexibility with regard to late domain position and interactions with host proteins (Elis et al., 2012; Wight et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies of extant gammaretroviruses.

claim: A dichotomous pattern of amino acid conservation was observed for the ERV-Fc NC proteins, with the N- and C-termini being poorly conserved while the central portion was well conserved.
source: A dichotomous pattern of amino acid conservation was observed for the ERV-Fc NC proteins. The N- and C-termini were found to be poorly conserved, while the central portion was well conserved.
evidence: This is based on amino acid diversity analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The essential ZF domains are located in the central, conserved portion of ERV-Fc NC proteins.
source: It is this central, conserved portion, where the essential ZF domains are located.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and amino acid diversity patterns.

claim: Residues with the greatest conservation in ERV-Fc CA NTD are present in regions that are known to be involved in intramonomeric and intrahexameric contacts.
source: This revealed that residues with the greatest conservation are present in regions that are known, from studies of modern retroviruses, to be involved in intramonomeric (Figure 3D) and intrahexameric (Figure 3E) contacts (Mortuza et al., 2004; Gitti et al., 1996; Kingston et al., 2000).
evidence: This is based on structural modeling shown in Figures 3D and 3E and supported by citations.

claim: Solvent-exposed amino acids (outside the betahairpin) in ERV-Fc CA tend to be less well-conserved.
source: In contrast, solvent-exposed amino acids (outside the betahairpin) tend to be less well-conserved.
evidence: This is based on structural modeling and amino acid diversity analysis shown in Figures 3D and 3E.

claim: The CA surface can be targeted by a variety of cellular antiviral factors, such as TRIM5α, TRIM-Cyp, Fv1, and MxB.
source: This may reflect either relaxed structural constraint or the fact that the CA surface can be targeted by a variety of cellular antiviral factors, such as TRIM5α (McCarthy et al., 2013; Ohkura et al., 2011), TRIM-Cyp (Sayah et al., 2004; Brennan et al., 2008; Liao et al., 2007; Newman et al., 2008; Virgen et al., 2008; Wilson et al., 2008), Fv1 (DesGroseillers and Jolicoeur, 1983; Kozak and Chakraborti, 1996), and MxB (Fricke et al., 2014; Goujon et al., 2013; Kane et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies of retroviral restriction factors.

claim: The pattern of amino acid diversity in ERV-Fc CA sequences is consistent with experimental mutational analyses of both MLV and lentiviral CA proteins.
source: Thus, this structural analysis shows that the pattern of amino acid diversity in ERV-Fc CA sequences is consistent with experimental mutational analyses of both MLV and lentiviral CA proteins (Auerbach et al., 2007; Rihn et al., 2013; McCarthy et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on comparison of ERV-Fc diversity patterns with experimental studies, supported by citations.

claim: The ERV-Fc pol gene encodes all the viral enzymatic functions, including the viral protease (PR), reverse transcriptase (RT), ribonuclease H (RNase H), and integrase (IN).
source: Similar to other gammaretroviruses and gamma-like retroviruses, the ERV-Fc pol gene encodes all the viral enzymatic functions, including the viral protease (PR), reverse transcriptase (RT), ribonuclease H (RNase H), and integrase (IN).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis of ERV-Fc pol genes.

claim: Very low diversity scores were observed across the majority of pol.
source: Indeed, we observed very low diversity scores across the majority of pol.
evidence: This is based on amino acid diversity analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Amino acid residues with high diversity scores in pol were primarily found near protease cleavage sites and away from catalytic active sites.
source: Amino acid residues with high diversity scores were primarily found near protease cleavage sites and away from catalytic active sites (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on amino acid diversity analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The viral env gene encodes the proteins responsible for binding to the host entry receptor and mediating fusion of the viral and host membranes.
source: The viral env gene encodes the proteins responsible for binding to the host entry receptor and mediating fusion of the viral and host membranes (Hunter, 1997).
evidence: This is established knowledge about retroviral Env proteins, supported by citation.

claim: Retroviral Env proteins are expressed as a single large polyprotein which is proteolytically cleaved into the surface (SU) and transmembrane (TM) subunits by cellular furin-like proteases.
source: Retroviral Env proteins are expressed as a single large polyprotein which is proteolytically cleaved into the surface (SU) and transmembrane (TM) subunits by cellular furin-like proteases.
evidence: This is established knowledge about retroviral Env protein processing.

claim: The resulting Env complex is a heterotrimer composed of three SU subunits and three TM subunits.
source: The resulting complex is a heterotrimer composed of three SU subunits and three TM subunits.
evidence: This is established knowledge about retroviral Env structure.

claim: Sequence diversity in SU is usually very high because even closely related viruses often utilize different receptors for entry and because SU is the major target of antibodies during the host immune response.
source: As even closely related viruses often utilize different receptors for entry, and because SU is also the major target of antibodies during the host immune response, sequence diversity in SU is usually very high (Katz and Skalka, 1990).
evidence: This is established knowledge about retroviral Env evolution, supported by citation.

claim: The extracellular region of TM is rather well conserved due to functional constraints including alpha helix formation, a conserved disulfide motif (CXnCC), and a highly conserved immunosuppressive domain.
source: The extracellular portion of retroviral TM proteins creates a series of alpha helices whose orientation shift dramatically during membrane fusion (Hunter, 1997). Gamma-like retroviral Envs also possess a conserved disulfide motif (CXnCC) involved in covalent interactions with SU, and a highly conserved immunosuppressive domain (Bénit et al., 2001). Due to these functional constraints, the extracellular region of TM is rather well conserved (Katz and Skalka, 1990; Bénit et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge about retroviral TM structure and function, supported by citations.

claim: The diversity within ERV-Fc Env sequences follows a pattern as would be expected based on prior knowledge of Env function; the SU domain displays extremely high sequence diversity, while the N-terminus of TM is well conserved.
source: The diversity within ERV-Fc Env sequences follows a pattern as would be expected based on prior knowledge of Env function; the SU domain displays extremely high sequence diversity, while the N-terminus of TM (where the alpha helices and the CXnCC and ISD motifs are located) is well conserved (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on amino acid diversity analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: All the ERV-Fc Gag sequences formed a monophyletic branch distinct from HERV-H and HERV-W.
source: The analysis revealed that all the ERV-Fc Gag sequences formed a monophyletic branch distinct from HERV-H and HERV-W (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Several clades consisting of ERV-Fcs identified in closely related species were identified, including Old World primates, New World primates, lagomorphs, and carnivores.
source: We identified several clades consisting of ERV-Fcs identified in closely related species, including Old World primates, New World primates, lagomorphs, and carnivores.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The ERV-Fc Gag phylogeny did not recapitulate the known phylogeny of the host species, with some clades comprising ERV-Fc from distantly related mammals.
source: However, the ERV-Fc Gag phylogeny did not recapitulate the known phylogeny of the host species – that is, some clades comprised ERV-Fc from distantly related mammals.
evidence: This is based on comparison of viral and host phylogenies, shown in Figure 4A and Figure 5A.

claim: Patterns where viral phylogeny does not match host phylogeny are suggestive of interspecies transmission.
source: Such patterns are suggestive of interspecies transmission (discussed below).
evidence: This is an inference based on phylogenetic incongruence.

claim: The consensus Pol sequences from Old World primates, New World primates, lagomorphs, and carnivores clustered together in the Pol phylogeny, similar to what was observed for Gag.
source: Similar to what we observed for Gag, the consensus Pol sequences from Old World primates, New World primates, lagomorphs, and carnivores, which comprise distinct clades in the Gag analysis, also clustered together in the Pol phylogeny.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: There were noticeable differences in relationships between the Gag and Pol sequences, indicating recombination events.
source: In contrast, there were also some noticeable differences in relationships between the Gag and Pol sequences.
evidence: This is based on comparison of phylogenies shown in Figures 4A and 4B.

claim: In the Gag analysis, the two distinct ERV-Fc lineages (ERV-Fc1 and -Fc2) represented in the ferret genome form a monophyletic clade, and similarly the ERV-Fc1 and -Fc2 lineages from the dog genome are most closely related to each other.
source: For instance, the relationship between the carnivore ERV-Fc1 and ERV-Fc2 lineages differed in these phylogenies. In the Gag analysis, the two distinct ERV-Fc lineages (ERV-Fc1 and -Fc2) represented in the ferret genome form a monophyletic clade, and similarly the ERV-Fc1 and -Fc2 lineages from the dog genome are most closely related to each other.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: In the Pol phylogeny, ERV-Fc1 lineages from the dog and ferret genomes are more closely related to each other, and separately the dog and ferret ERV-Fc2 lineages are more closely related, than between the two lineages from the same species.
source: In contrast, the Pol phylogeny supports a closer evolutionary relationship between ERV-Fc1 lineages from the dog and ferret genomes and separately the dog and ferret ERV-Fc2 lineages, than between the two lineages from the same species.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Incongruencies in topology between Gag and Pol phylogenies are an indication that recombination events involving different viral lineages took place between these two viral regions.
source: Such incongruencies in topology are an indication that recombination events involving different viral lineages took place between these two viral regions (examined further in the discussion that follows).
evidence: This is an inference based on phylogenetic incongruence.

claim: ERV-Fc lineages from Old World primates formed a distinct clade within the TM phylogeny, similar to both Gag and Pol analyses.
source: Similar to both Gag and Pol analyses, in the TM analysis ERV-Fc lineages from Old World primates formed a distinct clade within the tree.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Several TMs formed a monophyletic clade with HERV-W, including tarsier and a distinct subclade comprised of carnivore TMs (panda as well as dog and ferret ERV-Fc1).
source: However, other aspects of the TM phylogeny revealed a history of recombination events involving Env. First, and most strikingly, several TMs formed a monophyletic clade with HERV-W. These include tarsier and a distinct subclade comprised of carnivore TMs (panda as well as dog and ferret ERV-Fc1).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Two recombination events likely occurred that resulted in acquisitions of ERV-W Env by ERV-Fc: one leading to the ERV-Fc sequences found in the tarsier genome, and a separate event creating the chimeric virus that spread between several carnivore species.
source: Based on the evolutionary relatedness of the Gag and Pol sequences from these species, it is likely that two recombination events occurred that resulted in these acquisitions of ERV-W Env by ERV-Fc: one leading to the ERV-Fc sequences found in the tarsier genome, and a separate event creating the chimeric virus that spread between several carnivore species and independently endogenized each of them.
evidence: This is an inference based on phylogenetic patterns across different genes.

claim: The mouse and rat TM sequences share identity with ERV-Fc; however, these are found in the context of two unrelated betaretrovirus-like genomes.
source: Second, the mouse and rat TM sequences included here clearly share identity with ERV-Fc; however, these are found in the context of two unrelated betaretrovirus-like genomes.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and phylogenetic relationships.

claim: While the Gag and Pol sequences from lagomorphs consistently branched together, the TM sequences from rabbit and pika were most similar to the rat Beta-recombinant and aardvark TM sequences, respectively.
source: Third, while the Gag and Pol sequences from lagomorphs consistently branched together, the TM sequences from rabbit and pika were most similar to the rat Beta-recombinant and aardvark TM sequences, respectively.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The phylogenetic analyses argue for a long viral history of active exogenous replication during which time numerous recombination and interspecies transmission events occurred, resulting in the disparate topologies observed between the different viral protein phylogenies.
source: In summary, the phylogenetic analyses presented here argue for a long viral history of active exogenous replication during which time numerous recombination and interspecies transmission events occurred, resulting in the disparate topologies observed between the different viral protein phylogenies.
evidence: This is an inference based on the phylogenetic incongruencies observed across different genes.

claim: The tanglegram analysis revealed numerous incongruencies between the phylogenies of ERV-Fc Gag and their hosts.
source: This analysis revealed numerous incongruencies between the phylogenies of ERV-Fc Gag and their hosts.
evidence: This is based on tanglegram analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: A similar web of crossing lines was observed when the ERV-Fc Pol phylogeny was used in tanglegram analysis.
source: A similar web of crossing lines was observed when the ERV-Fc Pol phylogeny was used (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on tanglegram analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: There is evidence for cross-species transmission events between species of the same mammalian order (e.g. human and rhesus).
source: Figure 5A provides evidence for a number of cross-species transmission events between species of the same mammalian order (e.g. human and rhesus).
evidence: This is based on tanglegram analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: There is evidence for cross-species transmission involving hosts belonging to different mammalian orders (e.g. tenrec, lemur, dolphin).
source: However, we also found evidence for cross-species transmission involving hosts belonging to different mammalian orders (e.g. tenrec, lemur, dolphin), which is thought to be much rarer due to the genetic distances involved (Denner, 2007).
evidence: This is based on tanglegram analysis shown in Figure 5A and supported by citation.

claim: Several mammalian lineages harbored two lineages of ERV-Fc, including Great Apes, Old World monkeys, New World monkeys, ferrets, and dogs.
source: Additionally, several mammalian lineages also harbored two lineages of ERV-Fc, including Great Apes, Old World monkeys, New World monkeys, ferrets, and dogs (Figure 5A and Table S2).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: In each instance where a species harbored two ERV-Fc lineages, the molecular data indicate that the two lineages originated from independent cross-species transmissions and genome colonization events.
source: In each instance, the molecular data indicate that the two lineages originated from independent cross-species transmissions and genome colonization events in these species.
evidence: This is an inference based on phylogenetic relationships.

claim: The distribution of ERV-Fc in the mammalian species included in this study predominantly originated following cross-species transmission events of exogenously replicating viruses.
source: These findings indicate that the distribution of ERV-Fc in the mammalian species included in this study predominantly originated following cross-species transmission events of exogenously replicating viruses.
evidence: This is an inference based on phylogenetic and tanglegram analyses.

claim: A minimum of 26 independent cross-species transmission events resulted in the observed distribution of ERV-Fc among the mammalian species examined.
source: These observations in conjunction with other molecular characteristics of the viral lineages led us to estimate a minimum of 26 independent cross-species transmission events resulted in the observed distribution of ERV-Fc among the mammalian species examined.
evidence: This is an inference based on phylogenetic and molecular analyses.

claim: The estimate of 26 cross-species transmission events likely underestimates the total contribution of interspecies transmission to the spread of the exogenous virus.
source: However, this likely underestimates the total contribution of interspecies transmission to the spread of the exogenous virus because transmission may be more common between closely related species (e.g. due to genetic similarity of the hosts, or sharing of the same or similar range or niche).
evidence: This is speculation based on reasoning about detection limitations.

claim: ERV-Fc sequences in several mammalian clades reflected endogenization in a common ancestor with subsequent vertical inheritance by multiple descendant species.
source: Our data revealed that ERV-Fc sequences in several mammalian clades reflected endogenization in a common ancestor with subsequent vertical inheritance by multiple descendant species where they were sampled in this study.
evidence: This is based on analysis of shared orthologous loci.

claim: Mammalian clades showing vertical inheritance of ERV-Fc include the Great Apes (humans, chimpanzee, gorilla, orangutan); Old World monkeys (grivet, baboon, rhesus, cynomologous); New World monkeys (marmoset, squirrel monkey); and muridae (mouse, rat).
source: Mammalian clades for which this is the case include the Great Apes (humans, chimpanzee, gorilla, orangutan); Old World monkeys (grivet, baboon, rhesus, cynomologous); New World monkeys (marmoset, squirrel monkey); and muridae (mouse, rat).
evidence: This is based on analysis of shared orthologous loci.

claim: ERV-Fc was undergoing genome colonization between 30 and 10 million years ago (MYA).
source: Based on these findings and the reported times of speciation for these clades (Hedges et al., 2006), we inferred that ERV-Fc was undergoing genome colonization between 30 and 10 million years ago (MYA).
evidence: This is an inference based on speciation times and presence/absence of ERV-Fc in different lineages, supported by citation.

claim: The presence of similar or shared ERV-Fc2 elements among Great Apes must reflect infections that occurred prior to divergence from a common ancestor 15.8 MYA (orangutan/human split), but more recent than 19.9 MYA (human/gibbon split).
source: For example, the presence of similar or shared ERV-Fc2 elements among Great Apes must reflect infections that occurred prior to divergence from a common ancestor 15.8 MYA (orangutan/human split), but more recent than 19.9 MYA (human/gibbon split).
evidence: This is an inference based on speciation times and presence/absence of ERV-Fc in different lineages.

claim: Shared ERV-Fc1 elements among Great Apes indicate that this viral lineage endogenized apes between 15.8 MYA (orangutan/human split) and 8.9 MYA (gorilla/human split).
source: Shared ERV-Fc1 elements among Great Apes indicate that this viral lineage endogenized apes between 15.8 MYA (orangutan/human split) and 8.9 MYA (gorilla/human split).
evidence: This is an inference based on speciation times and presence/absence of ERV-Fc in different lineages.

claim: The New World primate ERV-Fc3-2 found in the genomes of the squirrel monkey and marmoset must be at least 19.1 million years old (marmoset/squirrel monkey split), but younger than 43.1 million years old (Platyrrhini/Catarrhini split).
source: Similarly, the New World primate ERV-Fc3-2 found in the genomes of the squirrel monkey and marmoset must be at least 19.1 million years old (marmoset/squirrel monkey split), but younger than 43.1 million years old (Platyrrhini/Catarrhini split).
evidence: This is an inference based on speciation times and presence/absence of ERV-Fc in different lineages.

claim: Both the ERV-Fc1 and ERV-Fc2 lineages in Old World primates were found in grivet, baboon, and rhesus, indicating an age of at least 11.7 million years.
source: Also, both the ERV-Fc1 and ERV-Fc2 lineages in Old World primates were found in grivet, baboon, and rhesus, indicating an age of at least 11.7 million years, but additional data indicated that these lineages are also present in colobine monkeys [Patel, Senter, Johnson & Diehl, personal communication], pushing this this date back to 17.1 MYA, but no later than 29.1 MYA (Hominoidae/Cercopithecidae split).
evidence: This is an inference based on speciation times and presence/absence of ERV-Fc in different lineages, including unpublished data.

claim: The ERV-Fcs present in mice and rat genomes pre-date speciation (22.6 MYA) but are not found in hamsters (43 MYA).
source: Finally, the ERV-Fcs present in mice and rat genomes pre-date speciation (22.6 MYA) but are not found in hamsters (43 MYA).
evidence: This is based on presence/absence of ERV-Fc in different rodent lineages and speciation times.

claim: The oldest ERV-Fc loci are the ERV-Fc2 elements in the genomes of ferret and canine, which date to 35.2 and 32.4 MYA, respectively.
source: Regarding the first point, the oldest ERV-Fc loci are the ERV-Fc2 elements in the genomes of ferret and canine, which date to 35.2 and 32.4 MYA, respectively.
evidence: This is based on LTR divergence molecular clock analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: ERV-Fc3-2 isolates from the squirrel monkey and marmoset genomes have oldest loci dating to 31.3 and 29.3 MYA, respectively.
source: Nearly as old are ERV-Fc3-2 isolates from the squirrel monkey and marmoset genomes, whose oldest loci date to 31.3 and 29.3 MYA, respectively.
evidence: This is based on LTR divergence molecular clock analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The squirrel monkey and marmoset diverged from a common ancestor approximately 19 MYA, and they share many orthologous ERV-Fc3-2 loci.
source: These species diverged from a common ancestor approximately 19 MYA, and they share many orthologous ERV-Fc3-2 loci.
evidence: This is based on analysis of shared loci and known speciation times.

claim: The LTR-based molecular clock calculations on ERV-Fc3-2 loci yield age estimates consistent with age estimates based on species divergence times.
source: Importantly, the LTR-based molecular clock calculations on these ERV-Fc3-2 loci yield age estimates consistent with age estimates based on species divergence times.
evidence: This is based on comparison of two independent dating methods.

claim: Several species harbor ERV-Fc isolates whose oldest loci date to around 20 MYA, including rabbit, human (HERV-Fc2), squirrel monkey (ERV-Fc3-1), marmoset (ERV-Fc3-1), and dog (ERV-Fc1).
source: Several species harbor ERV-Fc isolates whose oldest loci date to around 20 MYA. This group includes rabbit, human (HERV-Fc2), squirrel monkey (ERV-Fc3-1), marmoset (ERV-Fc3-1), and dog (ERV-Fc1).
evidence: This is based on LTR divergence molecular clock analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Significant cross-species transmission and endogenization by ERV-Fc took place over a span of more than 10 million years.
source: Thus, our data showed that significant cross-species transmission and endogenization by ERV-Fc took place over a span of more than 10 million years.
evidence: This is based on the range of ages estimated for ERV-Fc loci across different species.

claim: For nearly every species' genome that contained multiple ERV-Fc integrations, the difference in age between the oldest locus and the youngest locus was greater than 10 million years.
source: For example, for nearly every species' genome that contained multiple ERV-Fc integrations, the difference in age between the oldest locus and the youngest locus was greater than 10 million years.
evidence: This is based on LTR divergence molecular clock analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The younger ERV-Fc loci displayed features known to correlate with expansion by post-insertion amplification mechanisms, including large deletions of the viral genes.
source: In addition, the younger loci displayed features known to correlate with expansion by post-insertion amplification mechanisms, including large deletions of the viral genes (Magiorkinis et al., 2012), while the older loci tended to retain recognizable gag, pol, and env sequences [68 and data not shown].
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and supported by citation.

claim: ERV-Fc2 sequences encode a canonical ERV-Fc Env, are found in the cat, dog, and ferret genomes, and appeared in the genomes of the ancestors of dogs and ferrets very early in the history of ERV-Fc.
source: ERV-Fc2 sequences encode a canonical ERV-Fc Env (Figure 4C), are found in the cat, dog, and ferret genomes, and appeared in the genomes of the ancestors of dogs and ferrets very early in the history of ERV-Fc (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis (Figure 4C) and age estimates (Figure 5B).

claim: ERV-Fc1 elements encode an Env most similar to ERV-W, are present in the genomes of giant pandas, dogs, and ferrets, and colonized the ancestors of dogs and ferrets >10 million years after ERV-Fc2.
source: In contrast, ERV-Fc1 elements encode an Env most similar to ERV-W (Figure 4C), are present in the genomes of giant pandas, dogs, and ferrets, and colonized the ancestors of dogs and ferrets >10 million years after ERV-Fc2 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis (Figure 4C) and age estimates (Figure 5B).

claim: There is an incongruency in the dog and ferret ERV-Fc1/ERV-Fc2 relationship between the Gag and Pol phylogenies.
source: Furthermore, we observed an incongruency in the dog and ferret ERV-Fc1/ERV-Fc2 relationship between the Gag and Pol phylogenies (Figure 4, panels A and B).
evidence: This is based on comparison of phylogenies shown in Figure 4.

claim: There is a clear ERV-Fc1 clade comprised of loci from all species known to harbor this recombinant ERV-Fc lineage (dog, ferret, and giant panda), and all canine ERV-Fc1 sequences reside in this clade.
source: First, there is a clear ERV-Fc1 clade comprised of loci from all species known to harbor this recombinant ERV-Fc lineage (dog, ferret, and giant panda), and all canine ERV-Fc1 sequences reside in this clade.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: There are three distinct ERV-Fc1 sublineages present within the dog genome that have distinct relationships with ERV-Fc1 sequences from other carnivores.
source: However, there are three distinct ERV-Fc1 sublineages present within the dog genome that have distinct relationships with ERV-Fc1 sequences from other carnivores.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: At least two, but more probably three, separate cross-species transmission events introduced ERV-Fc1 into dogs.
source: We interpret this as an indication of at least two, but more probably three, separate cross-species transmission events into dogs.
evidence: This is an inference based on phylogenetic relationships shown in Figure 6.

claim: The majority of the ferret ERV-Fc1 gag sequences form a monophyletic clade with gag sequences of the non-chimeric ferret ERV-Fc2.
source: However, the majority of the ferret ERV-Fc1 gag sequences form a monophyletic clade with gag sequences of the non-chimeric ferret ERV-Fc2.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: The observed phylogenetic associations are evidence that a recombination event replaced gag within the ferret ERV-Fc1 lineage.
source: The observed phylogenetic associations are evidence that a recombination event replaced gag within the ferret lineage.
evidence: This is an inference based on phylogenetic incongruence between gag and pol.

claim: All ERV-Fc1 pol sequences, including those from ferret, form a monophyletic clade.
source: This is supported by the observation that all ERV-Fc1 pol sequences, including those from ferret, form a monophyletic clade (data not shown).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis of pol sequences.

claim: A solitary ferret ERV-Fc2 gag forms a monophyletic clade with the canine ERV-Fc2 sequences.
source: Finally, a solitary ferret ERV-Fc2 gag forms a monophyletic clade with the canine ERV-Fc2 sequences.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: At least two distinct lineages of ERV-Fc2 jumped from another species into an ancestor of the ferret lineage: one potentially originating in a canine ancestor, and a second coming from an unknown source.
source: This likely indicates that at least two distinct lineages of ERV-Fc2 jumped from another species into an ancestor of the ferret lineage: one potentially originating in a canine ancestor, and a second coming from an unknown source.
evidence: This is an inference based on phylogenetic relationships shown in Figure 6.

claim: An initial recombination event allowed for the acquisition of an ERV-W envelope by a carnivore ERV-Fc-related virus.
source: Briefly, an initial recombination event allowed for the acquisition of an ERV-W envelope by a carnivore ERV-Fc-related virus.
evidence: This is an inference based on phylogenetic patterns shown in Figures 4, 6, and 7.

claim: Multiple cross-species transmission events resulted in colonization of the genomes of the ancestors of dogs, ferrets, and giant pandas by ERV-Fc1.
source: Subsequently, multiple cross-species transmission events resulted in colonization of the genomes of the ancestors of dogs, ferrets, and giant pandas.
evidence: This is an inference based on phylogenetic patterns shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Up to three interspecies transmission events account for the genetic diversity of ERV-Fc1 presently found in the canine genome.
source: Up to three interspecies transmission events account for the genetic diversity of ERV-Fc1 presently found in the canine genome.
evidence: This is an inference based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: Following introduction of ERV-Fc1(b) into mustelids, additional recombination event(s) took place with a pre-existing ERV-Fc2 virus, or viruses, resulting in the acquisition of the ERV-Fc2 gag.
source: Following introduction of ERV-Fc1(b) into mustelids, it appears that additional recombination event(s) took place with a pre-existing ERV-Fc2 virus, or viruses, resulting in the acquisition of the ERV-Fc2 gag.
evidence: This is an inference based on phylogenetic patterns shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: It was the double chimeric ERV-Fc1 that most successfully invaded the ferret genome.
source: It was this double chimeric ERV-Fc1 that most successfully invaded the ferret genome.
evidence: This is an inference based on the predominance of this lineage in the ferret genome.

claim: The origins of ERV-Fc date back at least as far as the beginning of the Oligocene epoch (~33.9 MYA).
source: Our analysis suggests that the origins of ERV-Fc date back at least as far as the beginning of the Oligocene epoch (~33.9 MYA).
evidence: This is based on age estimates from LTR divergence analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The Oligocene epoch was a time period of dramatic global change marked by the fusion of the African to the European as well as the Indian to the Asian continental plates, climatic cooling, development of vast expanses of grasslands, and the emergence of large mammals as the world's predominate fauna.
source: This was a time period of dramatic global change marked by the fusion of the African to the European as well as the Indian to the Asian continental plates (Briggs, 1995), climatic cooling, development of vast expanses of grasslands, and the emergence of large mammals as the world's predominate fauna (Prothero and Berggren, 1992).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Oligocene epoch, supported by citations.

claim: Evidence was found for ERV-Fc being present in species with little or no known geographic overlap at the early time in the viral life history, including musteloids, canids, Platyrrhini, and Tarsioidae.
source: However, we found evidence for ERV-Fc being present in species with little or no known geographic overlap at this early time in the viral life history, including musteloids, canids, Platyrrhini, and Tarsioidae.
evidence: This is based on the distribution of ERV-Fc and known biogeography.

claim: During the Oligocene epoch canids were restricted to North America.
source: The fossil record provides solid evidence that during the Oligocene epoch canids were restricted to North America (Munthe, 2005), musteloids were present in Asia (Sato et al., 2012), and Platyrrhini were likely restricted to South America (Bond et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to paleontological evidence.

claim: During the Oligocene epoch musteloids were present in Asia.
source: The fossil record provides solid evidence that during the Oligocene epoch canids were restricted to North America (Munthe, 2005), musteloids were present in Asia (Sato et al., 2012), and Platyrrhini were likely restricted to South America (Bond et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to paleontological evidence.

claim: During the Oligocene epoch Platyrrhini were likely restricted to South America.
source: The fossil record provides solid evidence that during the Oligocene epoch canids were restricted to North America (Munthe, 2005), musteloids were present in Asia (Sato et al., 2012), and Platyrrhini were likely restricted to South America (Bond et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to paleontological evidence.

claim: The previously widespread distribution of Tarsioidae, which were found in Africa, North America, Europe, and Asia, was contracting to its current geographic isolation in southeast Asia during the Oligocene.
source: The previously widespread distribution of Tarsioidae, which were found in Africa, North America, Europe, and Asia, was contracting to its current geographic isolation in southeast Asia (Gingerich, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to paleontological evidence.

claim: The geographic separation of host species, coupled with the clear phylogenetic relationships between their viral sequences, provides strong evidence for a rapid global spread of the exogenous forms of ERV-Fc.
source: The geographic separation of these host species, coupled with the clear phylogenetic relationships between their viral sequences, provides strong evidence for a rapid global spread of the exogenous forms of ERV-Fc.
evidence: This is an inference based on biogeographic and phylogenetic data.

claim: It is unlikely that musteloids, canids, Platyrrhini, or prosimians were solely responsible for the global viral spread of ERV-Fc.
source: Based on current phylogeographic knowledge of these early ERV-Fc hosts, and evidence for limited faunal exchange between these continents, we find it unlikely that musteloids, canids, Platyrrhini, or prosimians were solely responsible for this global viral spread.
evidence: This is speculation based on biogeographic constraints.

claim: The ERV-Fc genomic record in modern mammalian genomes likely represents only a fraction of the total exogenous viral spread.
source: Importantly, the ERV-Fc genomic record in modern mammalian genomes likely represents only a fraction of the total exogenous viral spread: for example, exogenous infections may simply have failed to leave an endogenous footprint in some species, and some unknown proportion of lineages bearing ERV-Fc insertions will have eventually become extinct (and the corresponding ERV-Fc record lost).
evidence: This is speculation about the incompleteness of the ERV fossil record.

claim: It is likely that the ERV-Fc 'fossil' record is incomplete, and that either extinct species or species lacking ERV-Fc sequences helped facilitate the worldwide spread of the exogenous virus.
source: Thus, it is likely that the ERV-Fc "fossil" record is incomplete, and that either extinct species or species lacking ERV-Fc sequences helped facilitate the worldwide spread of the exogenous virus.
evidence: This is speculation about the incompleteness of the ERV fossil record and potential intermediate hosts.

claim: After the birth of ERV-Fc, replication, cross-species transmission, and endogenization continued for approximately another 15 million years.
source: Finally, our results indicate that after the birth of ERV-Fc, replication, cross-species transmission, and endogenization continued for approximately another 15 million years.
evidence: This is based on the range of ages estimated for ERV-Fc loci.

claim: Active ERV-Fc reinfection may have continued until very recently in some lineages.
source: Our data, as well as other published reports (Bénit et al., 2003; Barrio et al., 2011), indicate that active ERV-Fc reinfection may have continued until very recently in some lineages, indicating that at least one ERV locus has retained functional gag and pol coding potential in those species.
evidence: This is based on the presence of young ERV-Fc loci and supported by citations.

claim: In ferret and canine, ERV-Fc1 acquired gag sequence from an older, pre-existing endogenous lineage (ERV-Fc2).
source: In ferret and canine, we found evidence that ERV-Fc1 acquired gag sequence from an older, pre-existing endogenous lineage (ERV-Fc2).
evidence: This is an inference based on phylogenetic patterns and age estimates.

claim: LTR dating indicated that in both dog and ferret species the oldest ERV-Fc1 locus pre-dates the end of active reinfection of the genome by ERV-Fc2.
source: Indeed, LTR dating indicated that in both species the oldest ERV-Fc1 locus pre-dates the end of active reinfection of the genome by ERV-Fc2.
evidence: This is based on LTR divergence age estimates shown in Figure 5B.

claim: It is plausible that there existed in the genomes of the ancestors of dogs and ferrets at least one functional ERV-Fc2 gag ORF that the newly introduced ERV-Fc1 could have acquired.
source: Thus, it is plausible that there existed in the genomes of the ancestors of these species at least one functional ERV-Fc2 gag ORF that the newly introduced ERV-Fc1 could have acquired.
evidence: This is speculation based on the timing of ERV-Fc1 and ERV-Fc2 activity.

claim: Observations in laboratory mice as well as in vitro and in vivo experiments provide several well characterized examples of recombination involving ERV sequences giving rise to replication-competent viruses with novel biological properties.
source: Observations in laboratory mice as well as in vitro and in vivo experiments provide several well characterized examples of recombination involving ERV sequences giving rise to replication-competent viruses with novel biological properties (Chong et al., 1998; Coffin et al., 1989; Paprotka et al., 2011; Patience et al., 1998; Telesnitsky and Goff, 1993).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.

claim: ERV loci could contribute to adaptive evolution of exogenous viruses by providing a reservoir of novel sequences that can be tapped into by co-packaging and recombination.
source: Thus, ERV loci could contribute to adaptive evolution of exogenous viruses by providing a reservoir of novel sequences that can be tapped into by co-packaging and recombination.
evidence: This is speculation based on known mechanisms of retroviral recombination and the observed recombination in ERV-Fc.
